idiom_name: Opaque (incomplete) struct type plus const-correct accessor functions
implementation_notes: C has no member access control, so the whole structure is hand-built as an abstract data type: the public header declares the handle as an incomplete type (`typedef struct circle_data circle_data;`) together with constructor, accessor and destroy function prototypes, and the definition of `struct circle_data` lives in the .c file (or a private header included only by the module), so callers can pass the handle around but cannot dereference it - the compiler rejects `c->radius` with 'dereferencing pointer to incomplete type'. Read access goes through functions taking `const circle_data *`, and because C's `const` is not transitive, an accessor that returns a pointer must return `const T *` (or a copy) or the caller can write through it. A private header is enough when several .c files of the same module must share the fields; for a strict invariant keep the definition in one translation unit.
pitfalls: `const` in C is not transitive: a `const circle_data *` still allows writing through any non-const pointer the struct exposes, so accessors must return `const T *` and the struct should stay free of exposed pointers.
Nothing prevents copying, casting or double-freeing the handle; provide a create/destroy pair and document ownership, because the caller cannot even see the struct to copy it safely.
Putting the struct definition in a shared private header gives every .c file that includes it full write access - the invariant then only holds by discipline.
Alignment and layout are part of the ABI once the struct is defined anywhere shared, so the opacity that was supposed to let the representation change can be lost again through a private header.
